newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Mandela says telecoms privatisation deal close.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says telecoms privatisation deal close.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela on Saturday said an historic deal to sell part of the country's telecommunications company to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium should be agreed in several weeks.
In a speech to businessmen during a five-day visit to Malaysia, Mandela said: "Intense negotiations are under way about important matters of detail."
"But without pre-empting these, we are confident that this relationship will be sealed in a matter of weeks."

The South African government announced on Monday that final negotiations for a 30 percent stake in the South African company would proceed solely with SBC Communications Inc and state-run Telekom Malaysia Bhd.
The government introduced legislation on Thursday to make it possible for the state-owned Telkom telecommunications corporation to sell the stake in April.
The amendment seeks to cancel a statutory prohibition on the sale of Telkom equity to more than one shareholder and to anyone other than the state.

Analysts have estimated the value of the 30 percent stake at over six billion rand ($1.35 billion), valuing Telkom at more than $4 billion, which they said would make it the largest privatisation in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Malaysia became the fourth-largest investor in South Africa last year -- behind more traditional partners Britain, Germany and the United States -- when the state oil firm Petronas bought 30 percent of listed South African oil company Engen Ltd .
The Telkom privatisation agreement "could not have come at a more opportune moment", Mandela told the Malaysian businessmen.
"For it is a practical reflection of an emergent strategic partnership between our two nations. And in many respects, it is a prototype of our multi-faceted relations."

"The large investment that the agreement entails; the transfer of technology and skills; the partnership between government and business; the social benefits to our communities; and the involvement of entrepreneurs from disadvantaged sectors of the population -- all these are experiences that Malaysia possesses in abundance."

Mandela has stressed on this last stop of his four-nation Southeast Asia tour that South Africa wants to learn from Malaysia, which shares with his country a common heritage as a former British colony with a multiracial population.

Some 25 years ago Malaysia adopted an affirmative action programme, including university quotas and preferential share allocations, aimed at giving indigenous Malays a leg-up in a business world dominated by ethnic Chinese.
At a press conference later on Saturday, Mandela was asked if South Africa would introduce quotas and affirmative action programmes similar to Malaysia's.

"It is our policy to ensure true affirmative action and that government institutions reflect all population groups," Mandela replied. "We will do that without introducing unfairness and injustice to the community that was in power."

Malaysia is the last stop on Mandela's four-nation Southeast Asian tour that also included the Philippines, Brunei and Singapore. He was to fly to Malaysia's resort island of Langkawi on Saturday before returning home on Monday.
Mandela is accompanied by a delegation of 115 ministers, officials and businessmen. He has also brought with him companion Graca Machel for the first time on a state visit.
